units.title: Proof habits and shape notation
outcomes: Translate a linear-algebra claim between prose, quantifiers, indexed sums and explicit shapes.
Prove an implication in both directions when needed, and identify where its assumptions enter.
Use contradiction, induction or a small counterexample rather than treating numerical tests as proofs.
units.why: A correct calculation can still answer the wrong quantified question. Proof habits make the assumptions behind every later decomposition and solver visible.

next.note: Use definitions to prove linearity and independence.
Apply quantifier discipline to asymptotic bounds.

study.title: Mathematics for Computer Science: proof templates and notation
study.locator: Lehman, Leighton and Meyer, Chapter 1, sections 1.1 to 1.9 (pp. 5 to 19); Chapter 3, sections 3.1 (pp. 42 to 45) and 3.6 (pp. 56 to 61); sections 4.1 to 4.4 (pp. 81 to 93)
study.depth: In Chapter 4, read the definitions of sets, sequences, functions and relations. Leave cardinality and the remaining logical-circuit material.

study.title: Induction and invariants
study.locator: Chapter 5, sections 5.1 to 5.3 (pp. 115 to 130), then 5.4.1 to 5.4.3 (pp. 130 to 136)
study.depth: Read the ordinary and strong induction templates and the robot invariant. Stop before the later state-machine applications.

study.title: Vectors, matrices and indexed products
study.locator: Chapter 2, section 2.2 (pp. 22 to 27), especially the indexed matrix-product definition on p. 22
study.depth: Use this as notation repair, not a second first pass. Treat a tensor here as an array with an ordered list of axis sizes; multilinear tensor theory is outside this unit.

focus: Declare domains before quantifiers. Negating 'for every \(x\), \(P(x)\)' gives 'there exists \(x\) with not \(P(x)\)', not 'every \(x\) fails'.
Separate an implication, its converse and its contrapositive. An iff requires both directions.
For \(A\) of shape \((m,n)\), write \((Ax)_i=\sum_j A_{ij}x_j\) with \(x\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Distinguish a scalar, a vector, a column matrix and an array with extra axes.
An induction proof needs a starting case and a step for every permitted index. An invariant needs initialization and preservation.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, prove that the columns \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) of a real \(m\) by \(n\) matrix \(A\) are independent iff \(Ax=0\) has only \(x=0\), using \(Ax=\sum_j x_j a_j\) in both directions. Then prove \((A^k)^\top=(A^\top)^k\) for square \(A\) and all integers \(k\ge 0\), starting with \(A^0=I\) and using the transpose-of-product rule in the step. As one NumPy check, create A=np.array([[1,2],[2,4]],dtype=np.float64) and z=np.array([-2,1],dtype=np.float64), with no random draws. Compute np.linalg.norm(A@z,2): the reference run gives 0.0, below 1e-12. The nonzero witness \(z\) refutes independence for this \(A\); the numerical check does not prove the general iff.
traps: Checking several vectors cannot establish a claim about all real vectors. One exact counterexample can refute it.
Swapping 'for every \(b\) there exists \(x\)' with 'there exists \(x\) for every \(b\)' changes solvability into a much stronger claim.
A vector of mathematical shape \(n\) is not automatically a NumPy (n,1) column. Write the storage shape separately.

selfTest.q: Where do the assumptions enter the independence iff proof?
selfTest.a: \(A\) has \(n\) columns in \(\mathbb{R}^m\), so \(Ax\) is the same linear combination used in the definition. Independence forces all coefficients \(x_j\) to vanish in the forward direction. In the reverse direction, the assumed trivial kernel forces the coefficients of any zero combination to vanish. Neither direction requires \(A\) to be square.

selfTest.q: Negate: for every \(b\) in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) there exists \(x\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(Ax=b\).
selfTest.a: There exists \(b\) in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) such that for every \(x\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Ax\) is not \(b\). This is one unattainable right-hand side, not a statement that every \(b\) is unattainable.

selfTest.q: Why does the transpose-power induction start at zero, and what does its step use?
selfTest.a: For square \(A\), \(A^0=I\) and \(I^\top=I\) establish \(k=0\). If the claim holds at \(k\), then \((A^{k+1})^\top=(A^k A)^\top=A^\top(A^k)^\top=A^\top(A^\top)^k=(A^\top)^{k+1}\). Squareness makes the powers defined; the induction hypothesis is used at the third equality.

selfTest.q: Is \(T(x)=x+c\) linear for a fixed nonzero vector \(c\)?
selfTest.a: No. Every linear map sends zero to zero, but \(T(0)=c\). Nonzero \(c\) is the assumption used to obtain the contradiction.

practice.name: 6.042J text: Problem 1.3(a), a bogus inequality proof
practice.note: Identify the first invalid step and repair the direction of the inequality. Then annotate the two linear-algebra proofs in reproduce with the assumption used at each step.

units.stopWhen: You can write the iff and transpose-power proofs without notes, negate the solvability claim with the domains intact, and explain why the NumPy witness is a refutation rather than a universal proof.

fit.note: The proof companion supplies checked templates and a named proof-debugging problem; MML supplies the matrix notation. Narrowed readings keep this within six hours.

units.title: Linear maps, span, independence and change of basis
outcomes: Construct a matrix representation from the images of an ordered basis and derive the matrix for a composition.
Distinguish spanning, independence and being a basis, including uniqueness of coordinates.
Derive the change-of-coordinates formula with separate input and output bases.
units.why: Coordinates describe a vector; they are not the vector itself. Keeping that distinction prevents wrong transposes and explains why a better basis can simplify the same map.

next.note: Describe what the map reaches and what it loses.
Apply the distinction between the map and its coordinate representation.

study.title: Independence and matrix representations
study.locator: Video Lecture 9, Independence, basis, and dimension; Lecture 30, Linear transformations and their matrices; Lecture 31, Change of basis; image compression
study.depth: In Lecture 31, stop after change of basis; leave image compression for SVD. These are video numbers, not calendar session numbers.

study.title: Basis change as a composition
study.locator: Chapter 2, sections 2.5 to 2.6 (pp. 40 to 48) for definitions, then 2.7.1 to 2.7.2 (pp. 50 to 58), especially Theorem 2.20 and its proof on pp. 54 to 55
study.depth: Read the basis-change proof line by line. Leave kernel/image in 2.7.3 for the next unit.

focus: Spanning gives existence of coordinates; independence gives uniqueness. Both are needed for a basis.
Column \(j\) is the output coordinate vector of the image of input basis vector \(j\). Composition acts right to left on column vectors.

If \(x_{\text{old}}=Sx_{\text{new}}\) and \(y_{\text{old}}=Ty_{\text{new}}\), then the new representation is \(T^{-1}AS\). Only an endomorphism with the same basis change at both ends gives \(S^{-1}AS\).
units.reproduce: Derive \(T^{-1}AS\) by following coordinates through three maps. By hand take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), \(S=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(T=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and obtain \(C=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\-2&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). For new input \(z=(1,2)\), compute old input \((3,2)\), old output \((6,2)\), and new output \((6,-4)\). Check once in NumPy: create these arrays with dtype=np.float64, without random draws; compute C=np.linalg.solve(T,A@S) and np.linalg.norm(T@(C@z)-A@(S@z),2). The reference difference is 0.0; require it below 1e-12 rather than asserting floating-point equality.
traps: \(S\) contains the new basis vectors in old coordinates, not the reverse conversion. The inverse belongs on the output conversion.
A spanning list may contain redundant vectors. Its coefficients need not be unique.
An affine map with a nonzero offset is not a linear map even when implemented with a matrix multiplication.

selfTest.q: Why does a basis give unique coordinates?
selfTest.a: Spanning gives at least one expansion. Subtracting two expansions gives a zero linear combination. Independence forces every difference of coefficients to be zero. The two basis assumptions are used in different steps.

selfTest.q: For \(f(x)=Ax\) and \(g(y)=By\), which matrix represents \(g\) composed with \(f\)?
selfTest.a: \(BA\): \(g(f(x))=B(Ax)\). If \(A\) is \(m\) by \(n\), \(B\) must have \(m\) columns; with \(B\) of shape \(p\) by \(m\) the result is \(p\) by \(n\).

selfTest.q: Why is using \(S^\top\) instead of \(S^{-1}\) wrong in general?
selfTest.a: A basis matrix need only be invertible, not orthogonal. For \(S=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(S^\top=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), while \(S^{-1}=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Only orthonormal basis columns imply \(S^\top=S^{-1}\).

practice.name: MML Exercise 2.20: bases on both sides of a linear map
practice.locator: Chapter 2, Exercise 2.20(a) to (f), printed pp. 68 to 69
practice.note: Draw the two bases and solve the coordinate conversions before multiplying matrices. Part (f) checks the same output by two coordinate routes.

units.stopWhen: You solve Exercise 2.20 through its two output routes and can derive the order \(T^{-1}AS\) without memorizing it.

units.title: The four subspaces, rank and solution sets
outcomes: Find bases for all four fundamental subspaces and state their ambient spaces and dimensions.
Prove rank-nullity and the orthogonal-complement relations for a real matrix.
Describe every solution of \(Ax=b\) and distinguish existence from identifiability of \(x\).
units.why: Rank tells you which outputs are reachable and which parameter changes leave outputs unchanged. These are different failure modes, even before fitting data.

next.note: Project an unattainable right-hand side onto the column space.
Diagnose non-identifiable coefficients in an applied design matrix.

study.title: Null spaces, solution sets and the four subspaces
study.locator: Video Lectures 6 to 8, Column space and nullspace through Solving \(Ax=b\); Lecture 10, The four fundamental subspaces; Lecture 14, Orthogonal vectors and subspaces
study.depth: In Lecture 14, focus on row/null and column/left-null orthogonality. The norm and angle calculations belong to the next unit.

study.title: Rank-nullity and orthogonal complements
study.locator: Chapter 2, section 2.7.3 (pp. 58 to 60), Theorem 2.24 on p. 60; Chapter 3, section 3.6 (pp. 79 to 80)

focus: For \(A\) in \(\mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) of rank \(r\), column and left-null spaces live in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) with dimensions \(r\) and \(m-r\). Row and null spaces live in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with dimensions \(r\) and \(n-r\).
Prove rank-nullity by extending a basis of \(\ker(A)\) to a domain basis; show that the images of the added vectors form a basis of \(\operatorname{im}(A)\).
Each row dotted with \(x\) is a component of \(Ax\). This gives \(\ker(A)=\operatorname{row}(A)^\perp\); apply the same argument to \(A^\top\) for the other pair.
\(Ax=b\) is solvable iff \(b\) lies in \(\operatorname{col}(A)\). When solvable, its full solution set is \(x_p+\ker(A)\), so unique coefficients require full column rank.
units.reproduce: By hand use \(A=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&2&0\\0&0&1\\1&2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Find column basis \(\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}\), row basis \(\{(1,2,0),(0,0,1)\}\), null basis \(\{(-2,1,0)\}\), and left-null basis \(\{(-1,-1,1)\}\). For \(b=(3,4,7)\), obtain all solutions \((3,0,4)+t(-2,1,0)\). Changing \(b\) to \((3,4,8)\) makes the system inconsistent. Write the basis-extension proof of rank-nullity. Check once in NumPy with all arrays dtype=np.float64 and no random draws: matrix_rank(A) gives 2; the vector 2-norms of A@(-2,1,0), A.T@(-1,-1,1), and A@(3,0,4)-b each give 0.0, below 1e-12. The left-null vector dotted with \((3,4,8)\) gives approximately 1, certifying the hand inconsistency argument.
traps: Pivot columns must be taken from the original \(A\) to form a column-space basis. Row reduction preserves the row space and kernel, not the column space as a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
A tall matrix can have a unique solution for each attainable \(b\) without being surjective. Full column rank and full row rank answer different questions.
Numerical rank depends on a singular-value threshold. Do not confuse that decision with exact dependence in a symbolic matrix.

selfTest.q: Why are the images of the added basis vectors independent in the rank-nullity proof?
selfTest.a: A zero combination of their images puts the corresponding domain combination in \(\ker(A)\). Express it in the chosen kernel basis. Independence of the extended domain basis then forces all added-vector coefficients to be zero. Finite dimension permits the basis extension; linearity moves the combination through \(A\).

selfTest.q: When does a real \(m\) by \(n\) matrix give exactly one solution for every \(b\) in \(\mathbb{R}^m\)?
selfTest.a: Existence for every \(b\) requires rank \(m\); uniqueness requires rank \(n\). Both imply \(m=n=\operatorname{rank}(A)\), so \(A\) is square and invertible.

selfTest.q: Why is the full solution set \(x_p+\ker(A)\), not \(\operatorname{span}\{x_p,\ker(A)\}\)?
selfTest.a: Linearity gives \(A(x_p+z)=b\) when \(Az=0\). Conversely, any solution \(x\) satisfies \(A(x-x_p)=0\). The coefficient of \(x_p\) is fixed at one unless \(b=0\); scaling \(x_p\) generally scales \(b\).

selfTest.q: How can a left-null vector disprove solvability?
selfTest.a: If \(A^\top l=0\), then \(l^\top Ax=0\) for every \(x\). Thus \(l^\top b\) must vanish for a solution to exist. For the worked matrix \(l=(-1,-1,1)\) and \(b=(3,4,8)\), it is 1, a contradiction.

units.title: Inner products, norms, orthogonality and Gram-Schmidt
outcomes: Derive Cauchy-Schwarz and the induced norm, distance and angle from a real inner product.
Prove that orthonormal coordinates preserve inner products and lengths.
Implement Gram-Schmidt and check orthogonality, reconstruction and a dependent-column failure.
units.why: Orthonormal coordinates separate directions without mixing their lengths. They are the geometric foundation of projections, QR and spectral decompositions.

next.note: Use orthonormal columns to construct a projection.
Apply vector norms to clipping; leave optimizer exercises there.

study.title: Orthogonal vectors and Gram-Schmidt
study.locator: Video Lecture 14, Orthogonal vectors and subspaces; Lecture 17, Orthogonal matrices and Gram-Schmidt

study.title: Inner-product geometry and its inequalities
study.locator: Chapter 3, sections 3.1 to 3.5 (pp. 71 to 79), especially Cauchy-Schwarz, equation (3.17); section 3.8.3, Gram-Schmidt Orthogonalization (pp. 89 to 90)
study.depth: Use these definitions and the Gram-Schmidt construction to check the lectures. Leave function inner products and rotations.

focus: A real inner product is bilinear, symmetric and positive definite. Its induced norm is \(\sqrt{<x,x>}\); angles require both vectors to be nonzero.
For \(y\) nonzero, expand the nonnegative squared norm of \(x-(<x,y>/<y,y>)y\) to derive Cauchy-Schwarz. Handle \(y=0\) separately.
Gram-Schmidt subtracts components in previously accepted directions and then normalizes. Independence is what prevents a zero residual in exact arithmetic.
For tall \(Q\) with \(Q^\top Q=I\), lengths are preserved in the coordinate-to-vector map. \(QQ^\top\) need not be the identity.
units.reproduce: Derive Cauchy-Schwarz from the nonnegative squared norm, then work MML Exercise 3.8 by hand: \(b_1=(1,1,1)\), \(b_2=(-1,2,0)\) give \(q_1=(1,1,1)/\sqrt{3}\), \(q_2=(-4,5,-1)/\sqrt{42}\). Implement modified Gram-Schmidt for A=np.array([[1,-1],[1,2],[1,0]],dtype=np.float64), with no random draws: for each column v, sequentially set R[i,j]=Q[:,i]@v and v-=R[i,j]*Q[:,i], then R[j,j]=norm(v,2) and Q[:,j]=v/R[j,j]. Reject a residual norm \(\le 10^{-12}\) on this small scale. Check the Frobenius norms of Q.T@Q-I and A-Q@R; the reference run gives 3.6e-16 and 2.2e-16. Against Qref=np.linalg.qr(A,mode='reduced')[0], the projector difference norm(Q@Q.T-Qref@Qref.T,'fro') is 5.1e-16. Require all three below 1e-12. Replacing \(b_2\) by \(2b_1\) must trigger the dependence guard.
traps: Orthogonal vectors are not necessarily unit vectors. Projection coefficients need division by their squared lengths unless they are normalized.
Normalizing a zero or numerically tiny Gram-Schmidt residual produces invalid or unreliable columns. A fixed threshold is only appropriate to the stated scale.
Comparing \(Q\) columns directly with a library QR ignores valid sign changes. Compare spans through projectors and check your own reconstruction.

selfTest.q: Where does positive definiteness enter Cauchy-Schwarz?
selfTest.a: For \(y\) nonzero it gives \(<y,y>>0\), permitting division. The squared residual is nonnegative, yielding \(<x,y>^2\le <x,x><y,y>\). Equality requires the residual to be zero, again by positive definiteness. For \(y=0\) both sides are zero.

selfTest.q: How does Cauchy-Schwarz imply the triangle inequality?
selfTest.a: Expand \(\|x+y\|^2=\|x\|^2+2<x,y>+\|y\|^2\) and bound \(<x,y>\le\|x\|\|y\|\). This is at most \((\|x\|+\|y\|)^2\). Both sides are nonnegative, so taking square roots preserves the inequality.

selfTest.q: Why does Gram-Schmidt keep the same span at every step?
selfTest.a: The new residual is the current input minus a combination of earlier outputs, so it lies in the enlarged input span. Conversely the input is that residual plus earlier outputs. Independence makes the residual nonzero, so normalization changes neither span. The first nonzero input establishes the base case.

selfTest.q: For \(Q\) of shape 3 by 2 with orthonormal columns, why is \(QQ^\top\) not \(I_3\)?
selfTest.a: Its image has dimension two and it annihilates the one-dimensional orthogonal complement. \(I_3\) has rank three. \(Q^\top Q=I_2\) still implies \(\|Qz\|_2=\|z\|_2\) for \(z\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

units.title: Projections, residuals and least squares
outcomes: Derive the normal equations from residual orthogonality, without differentiating a loss.
Prove symmetry and idempotence of an orthogonal projection and explain uniqueness of the fitted vector.
Implement projection and a full-column-rank least-squares solve using QR with shape and residual checks.
units.why: Least squares is a geometric approximation before it is a statistical estimator. That geometry explains both the normal equations and why a correct formula need not be the right computational method.

next.note: Apply this derivation to solver choice on an ill-conditioned design.
Remove the full-column-rank restriction with the pseudoinverse.

study.title: Projection matrices and least squares
study.locator: Video Lecture 15, Projections onto subspaces; Lecture 16, Projection matrices and least squares

study.title: Least squares via QR
study.locator: Chapter 12, sections 12.1 to 12.3, printed pp. 225 to 234; Algorithm 12.1 on p. 232
study.depth: Read the solution and QR algorithm, not the application examples in 12.4. Implement a triangular solve, not an explicit inverse.

study.title: Alternative least-squares solution routes
study.locator: Lecture 9, Four Ways to Solve Least Squares Problems
study.depth: Compare the algebraic routes. Leave the near-collinear normal-equations-versus-QR experiment to Classical ML.

focus: Split \(b=p+r\) with \(p\) in \(\operatorname{col}(A)\) and \(r\) perpendicular to \(\operatorname{col}(A)\). For any other fitted vector \(p+d\), Pythagoras gives \(\|b-(p+d)\|_2^2=\|r\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2\).
Residual orthogonality gives \(A^\top(b-Ax)=0\). Full column rank makes \(A^\top A\) invertible and the coefficient solution unique.
\(P=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\) is a derivation formula. With an orthonormal column basis \(Q\), compute \(P=QQ^\top\) and solve \(Rx=Q^\top b\).
\(P^2=P\) expresses projecting twice; \(P^\top=P\) expresses orthogonality. Idempotence alone allows oblique projections.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the Pythagorean minimization argument, normal equations, \(P^\top=P\) and \(P^2=P\). For \(A=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) and \(b=(1,0,0)\), work by hand to get \(x=(2/3,-1/3)\), residual \((1/3,-1/3,1/3)\), and \(P=\frac{1}{3}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1&-1\\1&2&1\\-1&1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Implement the NumPy check with A and b as float64 arrays, no random draws: Q,R=np.linalg.qr(A,mode='reduced'); x=np.linalg.solve(R,Q.T@b); P=Q@Q.T. Measure norm(P-P_hand,'fro'), norm(P@P-P,'fro'), norm(P.T-P,'fro'), and norm(A.T@(b-A@x),2). The reference values are 5.7e-16, 5.7e-16, 0.0 and 5.5e-16; require each below 1e-12. The squared residual norm is approximately 0.3333333333333334, within 1e-12 of 1/3.
traps: A small residual is not required at the optimum: an unattainable \(b\) leaves a nonzero orthogonal residual. Test \(A^\top r\) as well.
Rank deficiency leaves the fitted vector unique but may leave infinitely many coefficient vectors. The inverse formula is then undefined.
For \(P=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), \(P^2=P\) but \(P^\top\) is not \(P\). It is not the nearest-point Euclidean projection.

selfTest.q: Why is the orthogonal projection the unique nearest fitted vector?
selfTest.a: Every alternative differs by \(d\) in the subspace. Orthogonality makes \(r^\top d=0\), so its squared error is \(\|r\|^2+\|d\|^2\). Positive definiteness makes the extra term positive unless \(d=0\). No column-rank assumption is needed for uniqueness of the fitted vector.

selfTest.q: Where is full column rank used in deriving the inverse formula?
selfTest.a: For nonzero \(z\), independence gives \(Az\) nonzero, so \(z^\top A^\top Az=\|Az\|^2>0\). Thus \(A^\top A\) is invertible. Residual orthogonality gives normal equations even without this assumption.

selfTest.q: Why do symmetry and idempotence together imply an orthogonal projection?
selfTest.a: Idempotence fixes every vector in \(\operatorname{im}(P)\) and puts \((I-P)b\) in \(\ker(P)\). For \(Pu\) in \(\operatorname{im}(P)\) and \(z\) in \(\ker(P)\), symmetry gives \((Pu)^\top z=u^\top Pz=0\). Thus the two pieces are orthogonal; neither condition alone supplies both facts.

selfTest.q: For full-column-rank \(A=QR\), why solve \(Rx=Q^\top b\)?
selfTest.a: \(Q^\top(b-QRx)=0\) follows from residual orthogonality. \(Q^\top Q=I\) reduces it to \(Rx=Q^\top b\). Full column rank makes square triangular \(R\) invertible. This avoids forming \(A^\top A\).

units.title: Eigenvalues, symmetric and positive-semidefinite matrices
outcomes: Derive a symmetric eigendecomposition and explain why a general square matrix may not diagonalize.
Give the spectral-theorem induction argument, including the invariant orthogonal complement.
Prove the eigenvalue test for PSD and the Gram-matrix singularity criterion.
units.why: Symmetry turns a matrix into independent orthogonal directions. The signs of its eigenvalues then decide whether its quadratic form is a valid squared length or has a downhill direction.

next.note: Apply the spectral theorem to \(A^\top A\) to construct an SVD.
Use PSD geometry to understand ridge's shifted Gram spectrum.
Apply spectral and variance reasoning to signal propagation.

study.locator: Video Lectures 21 and 22, Eigenvalues and eigenvectors and Diagonalization and powers of A; Lecture 25, Symmetric matrices and positive definiteness; Lecture 27, Positive definite matrices and minima
study.depth: Focus Lecture 25 on real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; learn the conjugate-transpose argument even though the worked matrices are real. In Lecture 27, focus on quadratic-form tests, not optimization applications.

study.title: Gram matrices and the spectral theorem
study.locator: Chapter 4, section 4.2, Theorems 4.14 and 4.15 on p. 111 and Example 4.8 on pp. 111 to 112; section 4.4 (pp. 115 to 119)
study.depth: Check the Gram proof line by line. For repeated eigenvalues, distinguish an orthonormal eigenbasis that exists from an arbitrary basis returned for the eigenspace. Leave Jordan form.

study.title: Positive definite and semidefinite matrices
study.locator: Lecture 5, Positive Definite and Semidefinite Matrices

focus: A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Distinct eigenvalues imply orthogonality; repeated eigenvalues require choosing an orthonormal basis within the eigenspace.
Complete the spectral-theorem proof by showing that the complement of one unit eigenvector is invariant under \(A\), then induct on dimension. State the eigenvalue-existence fact you use.
For symmetric \(A=Q\Lambda Q^\top\), \(x^\top Ax=\sum_i \lambda_i (q_i^\top x)^2\). PSD means every eigenvalue is nonnegative; positive definite means every eigenvalue is positive.
\(A^\top A\) is PSD since \(x^\top A^\top Ax=\|Ax\|_2^2\). It is singular exactly when \(A\) has a nontrivial kernel.
units.reproduce: Give the spectral-theorem induction proof using the steps in self-test, then derive the PSD eigenvalue test and the Gram singularity criterion. By hand diagonalize \(S=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\): eigenvalues 1 and 3, with unit eigenvectors \((1,-1)/\sqrt{2}\) and \((1,1)/\sqrt{2}\). Contrast it with \(J=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), which has only a one-dimensional eigenspace. Check S once in NumPy: S=np.array([[2,1],[1,2]],dtype=np.float64); lam,Q=np.linalg.eigh(S), with no random draws. Compute norm(S-(Q*lam)@Q.T,'fro') and norm(Q.T@Q-I,'fro'). The reference values are 6.5e-16 and 3.2e-16; require both below 1e-12, and lam within vector 2-norm 1e-12 of (1,3).
traps: A positive diagonal does not imply PSD: \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\) has eigenvalue -1 and its quadratic form at \((1,-1)\) is -2.
Invertibility does not imply diagonalizability. The worked \(J\) is invertible but defective.
The PSD eigenvalue test assumes symmetry. Do not classify a nonsymmetric matrix using only signs of its eigenvalues, or silently pass it to eigh.

selfTest.q: How do you complete the spectral-theorem proof, including its assumptions and base case?
selfTest.a: For \(n=1\) the real entry and unit basis suffice. For \(n>1\), the characteristic polynomial has a complex root by the fundamental theorem of algebra, hence an eigenpair \(Az=\lambda z\). Real symmetry gives \(A^*=A\), so \(z^*Az\) is real and \(z^*z>0\); therefore \(\lambda\) is real. A nonzero real or imaginary part of \(z\) gives a real eigenvector \(v\), which can be normalized. For \(w\) perpendicular to \(v\), \(v^\top Aw=(Av)^\top w=\lambda v^\top w=0\), using symmetry. Thus \(v\)'s complement is invariant. In an orthonormal basis its restriction is real symmetric of dimension \(n-1\); the induction hypothesis supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis there. Adjoin \(v\).

selfTest.q: Why are eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues orthogonal?
selfTest.a: For real symmetric \(A\), \((Av)^\top w=v^\top Aw\), so \(\lambda v^\top w=\mu v^\top w\). Distinct \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) allow division by \(\lambda-\mu\), forcing \(v^\top w=0\). This argument alone does not handle repeated eigenvalues.

selfTest.q: Why is PSD equivalent to nonnegative eigenvalues for a symmetric matrix?
selfTest.a: Symmetry supplies the orthonormal spectral decomposition. Nonnegative eigenvalues make every term in the quadratic-form sum nonnegative. Conversely, testing the form on each unit eigenvector gives its eigenvalue, so PSD forces each to be nonnegative.

selfTest.q: When is \(A^\top A\) singular?
selfTest.a: If \(Az=0\) for nonzero \(z\), then \(A^\top Az=0\). Conversely, \(A^\top Az=0\) implies \(0=z^\top A^\top Az=\|Az\|^2\), so \(Az=0\). Real Euclidean positive definiteness is used at the last step. Thus the Gram matrix is singular iff the columns of \(A\) are dependent.

study.title: PCA as a variance maximization problem
study.locator: Chapter 10, section 10.2 (pp. 320 to 325), equations (10.9) to (10.25)
study.depth: Use the spectral decomposition to bound the Rayleigh quotient; no optimization algorithm is needed. The book stores samples as columns. Transpose its convention for the row-sample NumPy check.

focus: For each positive eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) of \(A^\top A\) set \(\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}\), \(u_i=Av_i/\sigma_i\). Prove \(u_i^\top u_j=\delta_{ij}\). Zero eigenvalues mean \(Av_i=0\), not a vector to normalize.
For \(A=U_r\Sigma_r V_r^\top\), \(A^+=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^\top\). The row-space solution is orthogonal to all null-space additions, hence has minimum Euclidean norm.
For rank at most \(k\), Eckart-Young gives minimum spectral error \(\sigma_{k+1}\). The truncated SVD also has squared Frobenius error \(\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2\). State which norm you measure.

For centered row-sample \(X\) with \(n>1\), sample covariance is \(X^\top X/(n-1)\). A unit direction's variance is its Rayleigh quotient; right singular vectors maximize it, and retained variance is sum of retained \(\sigma_i^2/(n-1)\).
units.reproduce: Construct the SVD and pseudoinverse by hand for MML Exercise 4.8's \(A=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}3&2&2\\2&3&-2\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Singular values are 5 and 3; its rank-1 truncation is \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}5/2&5/2&0\\5/2&5/2&0\end{smallmatrix}\right]\), and \(A^+=\frac{1}{45}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}7&2\\2&7\\10&-10\end{smallmatrix}\right]\). Give the spectral-norm Eckart-Young proof from self-test. As one NumPy check, use float64 A, no random draws, and U,s,Vt=np.linalg.svd(A,full_matrices=False). Implement A1=(U[:,:1]*s[:1])@Vt[:1] and Ap=(Vt.T/s)@U.T. The reconstruction Frobenius norm is 1.2e-15; spectral and Frobenius truncation errors are approximately 3; norm(A@Ap@A-A,'fro') is 2.9e-15. Require identity residuals below 1e-12 and scalar errors within 1e-12 of 3. In the same check use centered float64 X=[[3,0],[-3,0],[0,1],[0,-1]], take its first right singular vector v, and reconstruct (X@v[:,None])@v[None,:]. Verify sample variances (6,2/3) and squared Frobenius reconstruction error 2 within 1e-12. Explain both results from the spectrum, rather than treating this as a fitted ML evaluation.
traps: Deriving existence from \(A^\top A\) does not recommend forming it to compute an SVD. Its conditioning cost is proved in the next unit.
Repeated singular values allow rotations within a singular subspace, not just sign flips. Compare reconstructed matrices or subspace projectors.
A numerical pseudoinverse must declare its singular-value cutoff. Inverting tiny retained values amplifies noise; never divide by zero and then mask the result.

selfTest.q: Why does the SVD construction cover rectangular and rank-deficient matrices?
selfTest.a: \(A^\top A\) is real symmetric PSD, so the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal domain basis with nonnegative eigenvalues. For positive values, \(u_i^\top u_j=v_i^\top A^\top Av_j/(\sigma_i\sigma_j)=\delta_{ij}\). For zero values, \(\|Av_i\|^2=0\). Complete the \(r\) output vectors to an orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb{R}^m\); \(m\ge r\) permits this. The identities on every domain basis vector then give \(A=U\Sigma V^\top\).

selfTest.q: What proves the spectral-norm Eckart-Young lower bound?
selfTest.a: For \(k<\operatorname{rank}(A)\), any \(B\) of rank at most \(k\) has a kernel of dimension at least \(n-k\). Its intersection with \(\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_{k+1})\) is nontrivial since the dimension sum exceeds \(n\). Choose a unit \(z\) there: \(Bz=0\) and \(\|Az\|\ge\sigma_{k+1}\), so \(\|A-B\|_2\ge\sigma_{k+1}\). Orthogonality in the SVD makes the truncated tail attain this bound. For \(k\ge\operatorname{rank}(A)\), choosing \(B=A\) gives zero error.

selfTest.q: Why does \(A^+b\) select the minimum-norm least-squares solution?
selfTest.a: In orthonormal output coordinates, minimize each reachable component by setting \(v_i^\top x=(u_i^\top b)/\sigma_i\) for positive \(\sigma_i\). Unreachable output components remain in the residual. The null-space coordinates do not affect the residual, but add their squared norm to \(\|x\|^2\). Setting them to zero uniquely minimizes the norm.

selfTest.q: Why must the unit-length constraint and centering appear in the PCA derivation?
selfTest.a: Centering makes \(X^\top X/(n-1)\) the sample covariance rather than an uncentered second moment. For unit \(v=Qz\), \(v^\top Cv=\sum_i\lambda_i z_i^2\le\lambda_{\max}\) since \(\sum_i z_i^2=1\). Equality is attained in a leading eigendirection. Without the length constraint, scaling a nonzero-variance direction makes the objective unbounded.

study.title: Norms and solver difficulty
study.locator: Lecture 8, Norms of Vectors and Matrices; Lecture 10, Survey of Difficulties with \(Ax=b\)
study.depth: Focus on the induced 2-norm, conditioning and loss of accuracy. Leave iterative and large-data solution methods.

focus: Write the contracted axes separately from broadcast batch axes. For a dense \(d\)-to-\(h\)-to-\(p\) map, shared parameters with biases total \(dh+h+hp+p\); retaining input, hidden and output for \(N\) vectors stores \(N(d+h+p)\) scalar activations.

The standard dot-product algorithm costs \(mn(2k-1)\) operations for an \(m\) by \(k\) times \(k\) by \(n\) product. Modified Gram-Schmidt QR costs about \(2mn^2\) for \(m\ge n\); optimized LU costs about \((2/3)n^3\) and each triangular solve about \(n^2\). These are algorithm-specific counts, not timing claims.

For invertible square \(A\), \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\). From \(\Delta x=A^{-1}\Delta b\) and \(\|b\|\le\|A\|\|x\|\) derive \(\|\Delta x\|/\|x\|\le\kappa(A)\|\Delta b\|/\|b\|\) for nonzero \(b\), using compatible induced norms.

For full-column-rank rectangular \(A\), define \(\kappa_2(A)=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\) over its \(n\) positive singular values. The SVD gives eigenvalues \(\sigma_i^2\) for \(A^\top A\), hence \(\kappa_2(A^\top A)=\kappa_2(A)^2\). Rank deficiency makes the Gram matrix singular.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the product count, triangular/LU loop sums, the fixed-\(A\) perturbation bound, and condition-number squaring from \(A=U\Sigma V^\top\). For a deterministic NumPy check, use float64 X=np.arange(24,dtype=np.float64).reshape(2,3,4), W=np.arange(20,dtype=np.float64).reshape(4,5), bias=np.arange(5,dtype=np.float64), with no random draws. Predict Y=X@W+bias has shape (2,3,5), Y[1,2,4] approximately 1018, and Y.sum(axis=1,keepdims=True) shape (2,1,5). The standard product count is 2*3*5*(2*4-1)=210 scalar operations, plus 30 bias additions, with 25 shared parameters. Then use A=diag(1,1e-6), b=(1,0), db=(0,1e-8), all float64; x=solve(A,b), xp=solve(A,b+db). Measure \(\kappa_2\) approximately 1e6, relative solution change norm(xp-x,2)/norm(x,2) approximately 0.01, and original-system relative residual norm(b-A@xp,2)/norm(b,2) approximately 1e-8. These attain the bound by design; use absolute tolerance 1e-12 for the two ratios and entry, and relative tolerance 1e-12 for \(\kappa\). This changes the right-hand side, not the solver.
traps: A successful broadcast can be wrong: subtracting a (3,) target from a (3,1) prediction produces (3,3), not three residuals. Assert shapes before arithmetic.
Array .T reverses all axes. For batched matrix transpose use swapaxes(-1,-2); transpose only the two matrix axes.
A small residual is backward-error evidence, not a guarantee of accurate \(x\). Conditioning belongs to the mathematical problem; stability belongs to the algorithm.

selfTest.q: What shapes result from (2,1,3,4) @ (1,5,4,6), and from swapping only the last two axes of the result?
selfTest.a: The matrix product is (2,5,3,6): 4 contracts and batch shapes (2,1) and (1,5) broadcast to (2,5). Swapping the matrix axes gives (2,5,6,3). Reversing every axis with .T would instead give (6,3,5,2).

selfTest.q: Why does forming \(A^\top A\) square the 2-norm condition number, and which rank assumption is needed?
selfTest.a: The SVD gives \(A^\top A=V\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i^2)V^\top\). With full column rank all \(n\) eigenvalues are positive, so their extreme ratio is \((\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min})^2\). A wide full-row-rank matrix still has a singular Gram matrix, so the finite full-column-rank formula cannot be used there.

selfTest.q: Where is invertibility used in the perturbation proof, and why does a residual give the same bound?
selfTest.a: Invertibility lets \(A\Delta x=\Delta b\) become \(\Delta x=A^{-1}\Delta b\). Induced-norm inequalities bound the two products, and \(b\) nonzero permits relative normalization. If \(r=b-A\hat{x}\), then \(\hat{x}\) solves the fixed-\(A\) system with right-hand side \(b-r\); substitute \(\Delta b=-r\). No claim is made about the algorithm producing \(\hat{x}\).

selfTest.q: Why is reusing factors cheaper for several right-hand sides?
selfTest.a: For dense \(n\) by \(n\) \(A\), one LU costs about \((2/3)n^3\). Each subsequent right-hand side requires two triangular solves, about \(2n^2\) operations. Recomputing the factorization for every vector repeats cubic work. Pivot comparisons and data movement are not captured by these arithmetic counts.
